lesson.title: Read the Shape First: A Symmetry Checklist Before You Integrate
lesson.summary: Even symmetry, odd symmetry, and half-wave symmetry are three independent yes or no questions you can answer just by looking at a waveform's shape, and the answers tell you in advance which Fourier series terms must be zero, often before doing a single integral.
lesson.body:
Three separate geometric tests, covered one at a time in the last three chapters, can each be applied to any periodic waveform just by inspecting its shape. Even: does f(-t) = f(t)? If yes, every sine term (bn) is zero. Odd: does f(-t) = -f(t)? If yes, the DC term (a0) and every cosine term (an) are zero. Half-wave: does f(t + T/2) = -f(t)? If yes, the DC term and every even-numbered harmonic, both an and bn, are zero. None of these tests requires computing an integral; each one only requires recognizing a shape or a shift relationship, which makes them a genuinely useful first step before grinding through a full Fourier series calculation.

A waveform can satisfy several of these tests at once, and the effects stack. The square wave used throughout this chapter set is a clean example: it is both odd (confirmed in the Odd Symmetry chapter) and half-wave symmetric (confirmed in the Half-Wave Symmetry chapter). Odd symmetry alone would already rule out a0 and every an; half-wave symmetry alone would already rule out a0 and every even harmonic. Applied together, the only terms allowed to survive are the odd-numbered bn coefficients, which is exactly what the direct calculation found: bn = 4A/(n pi) for odd n, and nothing else at all.

To see that the three tests are genuinely independent, not just three names for the same property, work through a waveform that passes one test and fails another. Take a full-wave rectified sine wave, f(t) = A|sin(omega0 t)|. Because taking an absolute value folds the negative half of a sine wave up on top of the positive half, this waveform repeats twice as fast as the original sine; if the original sine had period 2 pi / omega0, the rectified wave's own period is T = pi / omega0. Test evenness: f(-t) = A|sin(-omega0 t)| = A|-sin(omega0 t)| = A|sin(omega0 t)| = f(t). Even, confirmed, so its series can only contain cosine and DC terms, no sines. Now test half-wave symmetry using its own half period, T/2 = pi/(2 omega0): f(t + T/2) = A|sin(omega0 t + pi/2)| = A|cos(omega0 t)|, which is never negative, while -f(t) is never positive; the two can only be equal where both happen to be zero, not everywhere. So half-wave symmetry fails, meaning this waveform is allowed to have a nonzero DC term and even harmonics, unlike the square wave. Confirm that directly by computing the DC term from its definition: a0 = (1/T) times the integral of A|sin(omega0 t)| over one period. Over its own period, sin(omega0 t) stays non-negative, so the absolute value bars can be dropped, and the integral of A sin(omega0 t) from 0 to T works out, after substitution, to a0 = 2A/pi, about 0.637A, which is nonzero, exactly as the failed half-wave test predicted.

Side by side, the two waveforms make the payoff of this checklist concrete. The square wave (odd, half-wave symmetric) has zero DC and only odd sine harmonics: a signal that swings symmetrically above and below zero with no ripple bias. The full-wave rectified sine (even, not half-wave symmetric) has a substantial DC term of 2A/pi and is free to contain even harmonics: this is precisely why a full-wave rectifier circuit produces an output with a real DC level plus ripple concentrated at even multiples of the input frequency, for example around 120 Hz for 60 Hz mains, rather than at the input frequency itself. That connection, from a geometric symmetry test straight to a real design consequence, is exactly what the DC Component and AC Component chapters build on next.
